characters.name: Hal Jordan
characters.tagline: Test pilot and independent-minded Green Lantern.
characters.bio: Abin Sur’s ring brings Hal into the Green Lantern Corps, where Sinestro becomes both mentor and adversary. Hal’s rejection of Sinestro’s rule of Korugar makes their conflict about power as much as personal rivalry. Emerald Twilight (1994) turns Hal into Parallax after Coast City’s destruction; Green Lantern: Rebirth (2004–2005) later explains Parallax as a separate fear entity possessing him. These are successive published accounts, not one unchanged original explanation. Rebirth restores Hal to the Corps and establishes the modern emotional-spectrum saga.

His failure to save Xanshi in Cosmic Odyssey becomes a lasting burden, alongside the loss of his wife and fellow Lantern Katma Tui. Later stories examine accountability and continuing to help others after catastrophe. characters.name: Kyle Rayner
characters.tagline: An artist carrying the Green Lantern legacy.
characters.bio: Ganthet chooses Kyle during the collapse of the Corps in Emerald Twilight. His imagination defines his approach to a power ring, while his early adventures explore inherited responsibility without the old institution behind him. Later he serves as Ion and leads Green Lantern: New Guardians. That series takes him through the emotional lights; his White Lantern transformation belongs to #16 (2013), rather than the opening twelve issues. These are successive roles, not powers he permanently retains in every later story.

The 2014 Sinestro series confronts him with what remains of his people and his army after Korugar’s destruction.

characters.name: Jo Mullein
characters.tagline: A detective with a different kind of power ring.
characters.bio: Jo brings experience with military and police institutions to a city whose official peace depends on suppressing emotion. Her investigation tests whether maintaining order is the same as protecting the people who live under it. Created by writer N.K. Jemisin and artist Jamal Campbell, she leads Far Sector (2019–2021), with letters by Deron Bennett. Her experimental ring recharges itself over time rather than through the usual external battery, but its available energy remains limited. That distinction creates real constraints during the story’s escalating crisis; “no battery” does not mean “cannot run out.” After Far Sector, Geoffrey Thorne’s Green Lantern (2021) brings Jo into the wider Corps ensemble. Following the Central Power Battery’s destruction, she investigates the attack while other Lanterns struggle without their rings. The move from one remote city to a Corps-wide crisis changes the scale of her work, while keeping her investigative role central. Her self-contained debut and later ensemble appearances are separate reading commitments.
characters.signature: An experimental ring that recharges itself, with a finite supply of energy available at any moment.

characters.name: Alan Scott
characters.tagline: The original Green Lantern, powered by a magical flame.
characters.summary: Alan Scott was the first hero published under the Green Lantern name, debuting in 1940. A founding Justice Society member, he channels the mystical Starheart through a ring and lantern. His Golden Age legacy is a distinct branch of the mythology, alongside the spacefaring Green Lantern Corps.
characters.bio: Alan Scott survives a sabotaged train wreck through the protection of a mysterious green flame. He fashions a ring from the lantern that holds it and begins a career as Green Lantern. Later stories call that magical power the Starheart and connect its origin to the Guardians, but Alan’s original heroic identity is not a Corps recruitment story. He becomes one of the Justice Society’s enduring figures and a mentor to later generations. His earliest adventures began in All-American Comics #16 (1940); his history subsequently crosses several versions of DC continuity. The younger Alan of the New 52 Earth 2 series is a separate incarnation, an avatar of the elemental Green rather than simply the same Starheart hero at an earlier age. Tim Sheridan and Cian Tormey’s Alan Scott: The Green Lantern (2023–2024) instead revisits the Justice Society hero’s past, exploring his hidden personal life and a mystery linked to his first love. Treat those retellings and alternate-world versions by their own series labels rather than merging every origin into one biography.
